prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets with endogenous prices, and models of dynamic industries, which made it possible to measure market power, mergers and welfare in real markets

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: a single part, B001, credited to Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. What changed is how I frame it after the exchange. I now tie the citation to a method-level unit: demand estimation with endogenous prices and equilibrium supply, plus the dynamic-industry framework. Production-function work and the wider new empirical IO programme stay as context and are not claimed. Chair Hassler's warning that widening the unit blurs the prize and reopens attribution persuaded me on this. I tested the case against the chair's question about a methods-and-tools contribution versus a substantive discovery. My criterion is whether a contribution (1) made something measurable that previously was not, (2) changed practice outside the originating community, and (3) survived long scrutiny. BLP-type estimation meets all three on the evidence cited in round 1. It yields counterfactuals for substitution, markups and merger effects that reduced-form work could not, and it has been used in antitrust, regulation, trade, health and environmental economics. It has had about three decades of replication, criticism and refinement. This is the standard I would apply to any field. It is the standard I would use for a measurement advance in my own discipline, such as a democracy-measurement dataset. A tool counts as a discovery when it changes what can credibly be said about the world. I also rely on the clarity of credit. The 1995 paper has three authors, and no other shortlisted entry divides as cleanly under a three-laureate cap. Support counts are not part of my case, and I do not treat the number of members who share this view as evidence of merit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that this is a toolkit prize. A Committee that reserves the prize for substantive findings about the economy could reasonably prefer B013 or B002 on that ground. The second reservation is the third slot. Bresnahan founded the new empirical IO programme and did early differentiated-product demand and market-power work. Choosing Levinsohn over him rewards the specific BLP result over the agenda behind it, and the citation has to make that choice explicit. Pakes's dynamic-games and production-function work is also only partly covered by a method-level citation. Applied BLP-type results are known to be sensitive to numerical implementation, instrument choice and functional form. I assess these from background knowledge, and I have not independently verified any citation, adoption or sensitivity claims.

responses.point: Krusell is the only member who names Bresnahan instead of Levinsohn. He argues that Bresnahan's market-power measurement and new empirical IO work are foundations of the programme the later toolkit made operational. He grants that a Levinsohn version would not be a scientific error. He also treated my earlier stance on Bresnahan as dismissive.
responses.response: I agree with the correction. Bresnahan's contribution is foundational for the question, and I should not have described it as merely adjacent. Our difference is the unit of the prize and not merit. If the citation is about the estimator, the credit goes to the authors of the 1995 paper and its inversion, and Levinsohn is a co-author of that result. A citation about the empirical-IO programme would move Bresnahan into the slate. If the Committee chose that framing, I would accept Bresnahan in the third slot in place of Levinsohn, and I would keep Pakes and Berry in both versions. I prefer the method-level version. It splits no jointly authored result, and Hassler's point holds that widening the unit invites contested attribution among Reiss, Benkard and Levin as well. I would regard either version as defensible.

responses.point: Enflo ranks B013 first and challenges my B013 judgment. She argues that Autor links the technology and trade strands, that the China-shock papers are over a decade old and have been tested, that debate has refined and not overturned the central patterns, and that a methods toolkit should not automatically outrank an empirical-conceptual contribution.
responses.response: I agree that a toolkit should not automatically outrank an empirical-conceptual contribution. My ranking rests on the three tests I apply to every candidate, and not on the toolkit label. I also accept that Autor links the strands and that the central patterns have been refined, not overturned. B013 would be a strong prize in a later year. My remaining reasons are about the credit boundary and how settled the evidence is. Dorn is a core author of the China-shock papers and is excluded under the three-name cap, so the Katz-versus-Dorn choice is a judgment call. The task framework also draws on authors outside the credited list, and magnitude and persistence questions are still active. B001 does not face these problems to the same degree, because its debates concern robustness of applications and not the existence of the core result. I do not regard the gap as large. I would not call a B013 prize an error. If a Committee settled on a single strand with a defensible trio, I would reassess it.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B001 first and B009 as his first alternative. He reads my B009 ranking as resting on coherent attribution among Persson, Tabellini and Besley. He argues that the 2024 institutions prize makes the overlap more than cosmetic and that cross-country identification in B009 is weaker than the tested methods in B001.
responses.response: Friberg's reading of my B009 ranking is largely right. I rank B009 as an alternative because its attribution is coherent and the achievement is distinct from the 2024 work. The 2024 prize rewarded evidence on how colonial-era institutions shaped long-run prosperity. B009 concerns how constitutional rules and electoral systems shape fiscal outcomes and state capacity. I presented the 2024 speech, and I do not treat that as evidence of what the prize should be. I agree with his methodological point. Cross-country identification in B009 depends heavily on assumptions, and I know from my own field how much measurement choices drive results there. That is why I keep B009 as an alternative and not as a lead. I also see a risk of treating B009 as the 2024 prize again, which is why I place it second behind a candidate with no such adjacency.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first and B001 as her first alternative. She argues that B001 is mostly a toolkit prize that committees weigh differently from discoveries, and that a two-name Autor-Katz award drops the trade-shock design. She says she would not support B001 over B013 only because it has more first-place rankings.
responses.response: I agree that first-place counts do not measure merit, and I have not relied on them. The discovery-versus-toolkit question is the one genuinely open issue. My answer is a measurement test. B001 created the capacity to recover substitution patterns and markups from market data, it changed practice in institutions such as merger review, and it has been scrutinised for three decades. For B013, I accept her point that the policy impact of the trade-shock design is large. The question for me is whether the Committee can name a stable trio for it. Her own file shows that the Katz-versus-Dorn choice carries judgment, and the Hassler and Krusell two-name versions show how unsettled the credit is. If members who prefer B013 can agree on a single strand with a defensible trio, I would weigh it again. I have no new evidence that would move me today.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee wants a method-level citation (Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn) or a programme-level one (Bresnahan in the third slot), and whether it would regard either choice as an attribution error.
Whether a measurement-capability contribution carries the same weight as a substantive empirical discovery, and where the Committee draws that line.

How far the numerical, instrument and functional-form sensitivities of BLP-type estimation would change a merger-review or welfare conclusion in practice. Evidence that would move me: replication or robustness studies showing that standard implementations give materially different counterfactual merger effects or welfare results. I have not seen such evidence in the supplied material.
Whether the dynamic-industry strand needs separate wording in the citation, since only Pakes of the three is credited for it.

Whether, if B001 is not chosen, B009 or B002 should take precedence. This is a judgment between overlapping adjacent prizes (2024 institutions for B009, 2022 banks and crises for B002), and a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore pair would be my version of B002.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from my profile and not adjudicated. I have no apparent tie to Pakes, Berry or Levinsohn, and none to the B002 names. B009 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) is close to my field of political science and political economy, but my profile names no collaboration with them. It is only an alternative. My long-time collaborators and V-Dem colleagues are not credited on any shortlisted entry. At Stockholm University I am a colleague, in a different department, of committee members Hassler, Krusell and Boppart. Hassler, Krusell and Boppart disagree about which configuration is best, and I did not defer to any of them. I delivered the 2024 presentation speech on institutions and prosperity. A speech prepared for the Academy does not establish a personal preference, and I do not treat it as a conflict. I have independently verified none of the evidence I use.
